## Introduction

The goal of this project is to understand how temperature heterogeneity within the city influences phenological events, such as the start of season (SOS) and end of season (EOS), of individual trees from various genera and species. To achieve this, I apply spatial statistical models as described below:

$$y(\mathbf{s}_i, \mathbf{t}) = \mathbf{x}_{\mathbf{s}_i,\mathbf{t}} \boldsymbol{\beta} + w(\mathbf{s}_i) + u(\mathbf{t}) + \epsilon(\mathbf{s}_i, \mathbf{t})$$

where $y(\mathbf{s}_i, \mathbf{t})$ represents the phenological event (e.g., SOS or EOS) at location $\mathbf{s}_i$ and time $\mathbf{t}$.

$\mathbf{x}_{\mathbf{s}_i,\mathbf{t}} = [1, \text{AvgTemp}_{\mathbf{s}_i,\mathbf{t}}, \text{AvgPrecp}_{\mathbf{s}_i,\mathbf{t}}, \text{AvgSrad}_{\mathbf{s}_i,\mathbf{t}}]$ is the vector of predictors, where each variable represents the preseason average (winter for SOS and summer for EOS, respectively).

$\boldsymbol{\beta} = (\beta_0, \beta_1, \beta_2, \beta_3)^\top$ are the regression coefficients for the intercept and covariates.

$\beta_1$ is the coefficient for the average temperature, which is the main interest in this study.

$w(\mathbf{s}_i)$ is the spatial random effect which accounts for spatial autocorrelation among locations

$u(\mathbf{t})$ is the temporal random effect which captures random year effect.

$\epsilon(\mathbf{s}_i, \mathbf{t})$ represents the residual error term.

This document adopts the same workflow for analyzing urban phenology data, with the key modification of **climate data source**. The aim is to provide a basis for discussion regarding the advantages and limitations of using different datasets (WU, Daymet and U-HAT) in urban phenology studies. New York City is selected as the case-study area for comparison. Phenological observations of individual trees derived from remote sensing are available for 2017–2024.

```{r}
#| include: false
#| eval: true
compare_climate <- read_rds("~/phenology-urban/data/proc/urban/NY/WU_surface/NY.rds")
```

## Data source comparison

Weather Underground (WU) data were obtained from the [Weather Underground program](https://www.wunderground.com/), drawing on multiple personal weather stations located within New York City. These data include daily measurements of temperature and precipitation. Since Weather Underground stations are unevenly distributed, I used INLA-based spatial models to interpolate Weather Underground station observations, allowing me to generate continuous climate surfaces and assign values to all individual tree locations.

Daymet data were accessed via the [Daymet](https://daymet.ornl.gov/), which provides gridded daily weather data at a spatial resolution of 1 km². For this comparison, I extracted daily maximum and minimum temperature as well as precipitation data for the same period (2016–2023).

U-HAT data were accessed from @uhat_climate, which provides urban air temperature data at large scales across the contiguous United States (CONUS) at a spatial resolution of 1 km². For this comparison, I extracted the day and night temperature and calculated the average temperature for the same period (2016–2023).

### Temprature

In this section, I compare the temperature data from three different sources: WU-interpolated, Daymet, and U-HAT.

#### U-HAT vs. WU-interpolate

The [@fig-compare-wu-uhat] below illustrates the direct comparison between the WU-interpolated data and the U-HAT data, focusing on the average seasonal temperature in each year. The first row shows the average winter temperature for the start of season (SOS) and the second row displays the average summer temperature for the end of season (EOS).

Overall, the UHAT tends to report higher temperatures and higher variance than WU in both winter and summer (as indicated by most points falling beyond the 1:1 reference line, and the wider range of point distribution). Also, WU data exhibit a greater number of outliers, which may reflect the variability and less standardized measurement protocols of personal weather stations. Therefore, I think UHAT is more reliable than WU-interpolated data in capturing thermal heterogeneity within city.

```{r}
#| label: fig-compare-wu-uhat
#| include: true
#| fig-width: 15
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Comparison of temperature data from Weather Underground (WU) and U-HAT for trees in New York City"
#| warning: false

wu_uhat <- compare_climate |> 
  select(id, taxa, year, temp_summer, temp_winter, UHAT_temp_summer, UHAT_temp_winter) |>
  st_drop_geometry()

plot_climate_comp <- function(data, x_label, y_label){
  plot_df <- data %>%
    group_by(year) %>%
    summarise(x_median = median(x, na.rm = TRUE), 
              y_median = median(y, na.rm = TRUE),
              x_p5 = quantile(x, 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
              x_p95 = quantile(x, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE),
              y_p5 = quantile(y, 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
              y_p95 = quantile(y, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE),
              .groups = "drop"
              )
  xy_range <- range(
    c(plot_df$x_p5, plot_df$x_p95, plot_df$y_p5, plot_df$y_p95),
    na.rm = TRUE)
  # xy_range <- range(
  #   c(data$x, data$x, data$y, data$y),
  #   na.rm = TRUE)
  ggplot(data, aes(x, y)) +
    geom_hex(binwidth = c(diff(xy_range)/25, diff(xy_range)/25), 
             alpha = 0.7, color = "NA") +
  # geom_point(data = NY_city_input, aes(x = temp_winter, y = doy),alpha = 0.5) +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Density",
                         limits = c(0, 3000),
                         trans = "sqrt",
                         breaks = c(0, 300, 1000, 2000, 3000)) +
    geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "grey80", linetype = "dashed") +
    scale_color_viridis_c(name = "Year") +
    coord_fixed(ratio = 1, xlim = xy_range, ylim = xy_range) +
    labs(x = x_label , y= y_label)
  
  # ggplot(plot_df, aes(x_median, y_median, color = year)) +
  #   geom_point(size = 0.5, alpha = 0.2) +
  #   geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = y_p5, ymax = y_p95),  width = 0.1, linewidth = 0.4, alpha = 0.1) +
  #   geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = x_p5, xmax = x_p95), width = 0.1, linewidth = 0.4,  alpha = 0.1) +
  #   geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "grey50", linetype = "dashed") +
  #   scale_color_viridis_c(name = "Year") +
  #   coord_fixed(ratio = 1, xlim = xy_range, ylim = xy_range) +
  #   labs(x = x_label , y= y_label)
}

wu_uhat_winter <- plot_climate_comp(
  data = wu_uhat %>%
    select(year, taxa, x = temp_winter, y = UHAT_temp_winter) |>
    filter(!is.na(x) & !is.na(y)),
  x_label = "WU winter temperature (°C)", y_label = "UHAT winter temperature (°C)")

wu_uhat_summer <- plot_climate_comp(
  data = wu_uhat %>%
    select(year, taxa, x = temp_summer, y = UHAT_temp_summer) |>
    filter(!is.na(x) & !is.na(y)),
  x_label = "WU summer temperature (°C)", y_label = "UHAT summer temperature (°C)")
```

#### U-HAT vs. Daymet

Similarly, I ploted [@fig-compare-daymet-uhat] below to compare the Daymet data and the U-HAT data. Generally, U-HAT reports higher temperatures and larger variance than Daymet in both winter and summer (as indicated by most points falling beyond the 1:1 reference line), which means UHAT could capture the urban heat island effect.

```{r}
#| label: fig-compare-daymet-uhat
#| include: true
#| fig-width: 15
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Comparison of temperature data from Daymet and U-HAT for trees in New York City"
#| warning: false

daymet_uhat <- compare_climate |> 
  select(id, taxa, year, Daymet_temp_summer, Daymet_temp_winter, UHAT_temp_summer, UHAT_temp_winter)|>
  st_drop_geometry()

daymet_uhat_winter <-  plot_climate_comp(
  data = daymet_uhat %>%
  select(year, taxa, x = Daymet_temp_winter, y = UHAT_temp_winter) |>
    filter(!is.na(x) & !is.na(y)),
  x_label = "Daymet winter temperature (°C)", y_label = "UHAT winter temperature (°C)")
    
daymet_uhat_summer <-  plot_climate_comp(
  data =  daymet_uhat %>%
  select(year, taxa, x = Daymet_temp_summer, y = UHAT_temp_summer) |>
    filter(!is.na(x) & !is.na(y)),
  x_label = "Daymet summer temperature (°C)", y_label = "UHAT summer temperature (°C)")

p_comb <- wu_uhat_winter + wu_uhat_summer + daymet_uhat_winter + daymet_uhat_summer +
  plot_layout(ncol = 2, guide = "collect") +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "a") &
  theme(plot.tag = element_text(face = "bold"))

ggsave(p_comb, filename = "~/phenology-urban/temp/figure_agu/temperature_comparison.png", width = 10, height = 9)
```

### Precipitation

In this section, I compare the precipitation data from WU-interpolated and Daymet.

#### WU-interpolate vs. Daymet

Overall, the Daymet precipitation data tend to be higher than the WU-interpolated data (as indicated by most points falling below the 1:1 reference line in [@fig-compare-daymet-wu]). However, WU-interpolated data show a wider spread, which could either capture localized heavy rainfall that Daymet overlooks or simply reflect outliers.

```{r}
#| label: fig-compare-daymet-wu
#| include: true
#| fig-width: 15
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Comparison of precipitation data from Daymet and Weather Underground (WU) for trees in New York City"
#| warning: false

daymet_wu <- compare_climate |> 
  select(id, year, Daymet_prcp_summer, Daymet_prcp_winter, wu_prcp_summer = prcp_summer, wu_prcp_winter = prcp_winter) |>
  filter(year < 2024)

daymet_wu_winter <- daymet_wu %>%
  select(year, x = Daymet_prcp_winter, y = wu_prcp_winter) %>%
  tidyr::drop_na() %>%
  group_split(year) %>%
  purrr::map(~{
    rng <- range(c(.x$x, .x$y), na.rm = TRUE)
    ggplot(.x, aes(x, y)) +
      geom_point(size = 0.2, alpha = 0.1) +
      geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "red") +
      labs(x = "Daymet", y = "wu",
           title = paste0(unique(.x$year))) +
      coord_fixed(xlim = rng, ylim = rng) +
      theme_minimal()
  }) |>
  wrap_plots(ncol = 7) + plot_annotation(title = "Winter precipitation for EOS")
  
daymet_wu_summer <- daymet_wu %>%
  select(year, x = Daymet_prcp_summer, y = wu_prcp_summer) %>%
  tidyr::drop_na() %>%
  group_split(year) %>%
  purrr::map(~{
    rng <- range(c(.x$x, .x$y), na.rm = TRUE)
    ggplot(.x, aes(x, y)) +
      geom_point(size = 0.2, alpha = 0.1) +
      geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "red") +
      labs(x = "Daymet", y = "wu",
           title = paste0(unique(.x$year))) +
      coord_fixed(xlim = rng, ylim = rng) +
      theme_minimal()
  }) |>
  wrap_plots(ncol = 7) + plot_annotation(title = "Summer precipitation for EOS")

daymet_wu_winter/
  daymet_wu_summer
```

## Summary

This document records the differences between climate datasets, to evaluate the suitability of each dataset and inform future data selection.

-   **Temperature**: Comparisons with both WU and Daymet show that U-HAT better captures urban heat island effects and fine-scale thermal heterogeneity, while WU is prone to outliers and Daymet underestimates urban temperatures. Thus, U-HAT provides the most reliable dataset for intra-urban temperature analyses.

-   **Precipitation**: Comparisons between WU and Daymet indicate that Daymet precipitation is generally higher, while WU shows a wider spread that may reflect outliers rather than true localized events. Since urban precipitation is less influenced by urban effects, Daymet provides a more reliable dataset with fewer outliers.

-   **Shortwave radiation**: Similarly, for shortwave radiation, where available data come primarily from Daymet and HUMID, I rely on Daymet for the same reason.

## Remaining questions

I still have two remaining questions regarding the UHAT:

-   Why does the number of points differ across dates? Is this related to the input imagery coverage or data quality control?

-   I used a MODIS/Aqua LST/E Daily L3 Global 1 km raaster map as a template and projected the seasonal aggregated UHAT data (in point format) onto it to generate raster maps. However, I noticed striping patterns along the latitude (e.g., horizontal lines at 41.0°N and 40.75°N in the @fig-example-uhat). Could this be an issue with my calculation method, or might it be related to the varying number of available points across dates as in the first question?

```{r fig-sp-inla}
  files <- list.files(r_output_dir, pattern = pattern, full.names = TRUE)
  coef_summary <- data.frame()
  # for one genus
  for (file in files) {

    species <- model_data$species
    # beta_names <- c("beta[0]", "beta[AvgTemp_mean]", "beta[Sum_mm_sum]", "beta[srad_mean]")
    # df_list <- lapply(seq_along(model_data$res$marginals.fixed), function(i) {

    #              density = model_data$res$marginals.fixed[[i]][,2], 
    #              beta = beta_names[i])
    # })
    # df <- bind_rows(df_list)
    beta_avg_temp <- model_data$res$marginals.fixed[[2]]
    
    coef_summary <- coef_summary %>%
      rbind(model_data$fix_effect)
  }
  
  coef_summary <- coef_summary %>%
    mutate(SigAlpha = ifelse(Sig == "*", 1, 0.2)) %>%

plot_coef_sp_city <- function(r_output_dir, phe_type){
  coef_summary <- read_rds(paste0(r_output_dir, phe_type, "_summary.rds"))
  p_coef <-  ggplot(coef_summary, aes(x = factor(Factor, levels = rev(Factor)), 
                               y = Estimate,
                               colour = Color)) +
    geom_point(aes(alpha = SigAlpha), position = position_dodge(w = 0.5), size = 3) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = Lower, ymax = Upper, alpha = SigAlpha), 
                  position = position_dodge(w = 0.5), 
                  width = 0.2) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Estimate") +
    coord_flip() +
    scale_alpha_identity() +
    scale_color_identity() +
    theme(legend.position = "right") +
    geom_text(aes(label = Sig, y = Upper + 0.05  ), hjust = -0.5, show.legend = FALSE) +
    geom_text(aes(label = Estimate, y = Estimate  ), vjust = -0.7, show.legend = FALSE, size = 3) +
    guides(alpha = "none") +
    # add title
    ggtitle(bquote(beta[Temp]~"for"~.(phe_type))) +
    theme_minimal()
  
  return(list(
    coef_summary_plot = p_coef
  ))
}
```

### MCMC, random group - most conservative

```{r}
#| label: fig-random-mcmc
#| include: true
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 21
#| fig-cap: "The distribution of the posterior of regression coefficients for `Temp~avg~` for each taxon group in New York city."
#| warning: false
#| eval: true

generate_mcmc_plot <- function(dir_path, coef, fixed_sp){
  process_files <- function(file_list, phe_type_label) {
    param_list <- map(file_list, function(file) {
      model_data <- readRDS(file)
      genus <- sub(paste0("(.*?)_", phe_type_label, "\\.rds"), "\\1", basename(file))
      if (fixed_sp) {
        param_data <- ggs(model_data$samples) |>
          filter(str_starts(Parameter, fixed("beta["))) |>
          mutate(beta_index = as.integer(str_extract(Parameter, "(?<=beta\\[)\\d+"))) |>
          filter(beta_index >= 5)|>
          rename(ParameterOriginal = Parameter) |>
          mutate(Parameter = genus)
          # mutate(waic = model_data$WAIC$WAIC,
                 mutate(converge = model_data$converge)
          #        milk = model_data$mean_logml)
      } else {
        param_data <- ggs(model_data$samples) |>
          filter(str_starts(Parameter, fixed(coef))) |>
          rename(ParameterOriginal = Parameter) |>
          mutate(Parameter = genus) |>
          # mutate(waic = model_data$WAIC$WAIC,
                 mutate(converge = model_data$converge)
          #        milk = model_data$mean_logml)
      }

      return(param_data)
    })
    combined_param_data <- bind_rows(param_list) |>
      filter(Parameter != "Alnus") |>
      mutate(phe_type = phe_type_label)
    return(combined_param_data)
}
  # Collect files
  SOS_files <- list.files(dir_path, pattern = "SOS\\.rds$", full.names = TRUE)
  EOS_files <- list.files(dir_path, pattern = "EOS\\.rds$", full.names = TRUE)

  # Process each type
  sos_data <- process_files(SOS_files, "SOS")
  eos_data <- process_files(EOS_files, "EOS")

  combined_param_data <- bind_rows(sos_data, eos_data)
  combined_param_data$phe_type <- factor(combined_param_data$phe_type, levels = c("SOS", "EOS"))

  # Summarize
  summary_data <- combined_param_data |>
    group_by(Parameter, phe_type) |>
    summarise(
      median_value = median(value, na.rm = TRUE),
      lower_2_5 = quantile(value, 0.025, na.rm = TRUE),
      upper_97_5 = quantile(value, 0.975, na.rm = TRUE),
      # waic = first(waic),
      converge = first(converge),
      # milk = first(milk),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    mutate(Sig = ifelse(lower_2_5 * upper_97_5 > 0, "*", ""),
           SigAlpha = ifelse(Sig == "*", 1, 0.2),
           Color = ifelse(median_value >0, "#0D0887FF" , "#FCA636FF")) 

  param_levels <- rev(unique(summary_data$Parameter))

  # Plot
  
  p1 <- ggplot(summary_data, aes(x = factor(as.character(Parameter), levels = param_levels), y = median_value,
                                 colour = Color)) +
    geom_point(aes(alpha = SigAlpha), size=3) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower_2_5, ymax = upper_97_5, alpha = SigAlpha), width = 0.4) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
    geom_text(aes(label = round(median_value, 3)),
              vjust = -0.7, size = 3) +
    scale_alpha_identity() +
    scale_color_identity() +
    guides(alpha = "none") +
    facet_wrap(~ phe_type, scales = "free_x") +  # flip x/y means free_x
    theme_minimal() +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Estimate") +
    theme(
      strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
      axis.text.x = element_text(size = 14)
    ) +
      coord_flip()

  if (coef %in% c("sp_effect", "z_hex")) {
    p2 <- ggplot(combined_param_data, aes(x = value, fill = ParameterOriginal)) +
      geom_density(linewidth = 0.1, alpha = 0.5) +
      scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-10, 10)) +
      facet_wrap(~ Parameter, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
      labs(
        x = paste0("Posterior distribution of ", coef),
        y = "Density"
      ) +
      facet_grid(Parameter ~ phe_type, scales = "free_y") +
      theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
      theme(
        axis.text.y = element_blank(),
        strip.text.y = element_text(angle = 0),
        panel.spacing = unit(0.4, "lines"),
        legend.position = "none"
      )
  } else if (coef == "spatial_effect") {
    p2 <- ggplot(combined_param_data, aes(x = value)) +
      geom_density(fill = "skyblue", alpha = 0.5) +
      scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-100, 100)) +
      facet_wrap(~ Parameter, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
      labs(
        x = paste0("Posterior distribution of ", coef),
        y = "Density"
      ) +
      facet_grid(Parameter ~ phe_type, scales = "free_y")+
      theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
      theme(
        axis.text.y = element_blank(),
        strip.text.y = element_text(angle = 0),
        panel.spacing = unit(0.4, "lines")
      )
  } else {
    p2 <- ggplot(combined_param_data, aes(x = value)) +
      geom_density(fill = "skyblue", alpha = 0.5) +
      facet_wrap(~ Parameter, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
      labs(
        x = paste0("Posterior distribution of ", coef),
        y = "Density"
      ) +
      facet_grid(Parameter ~ phe_type, scales = "free_y")+
      # geom_text(data = summary_data, aes(x = median_value-3, y = 0, label = round(median_value, 3)), vjust = -1, size = 3) +
      geom_text(data = summary_data, aes(x = median_value+3, y = 0, label = paste0("gelman.diag: ", round(converge, 4))), vjust = -1, color = "red", size = 2) +
      theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
      theme(
        axis.text.y = element_blank(),
        strip.text.y = element_text(angle = 0),
        panel.spacing = unit(0.4, "lines")
      )
  }
  p <- list(coef_summary_plot = p1, coef_density_plot = p2, summary_data = summary_data)
  return(p)
}

s_dir_path <- "~/phenology-urban/data/proc/model_output/final_models_Grid/mcmc/random_group_sp/NY/canonicalname/"
s_plot_obj_temp <- generate_mcmc_plot(s_dir_path,  coef = "beta[2]", fixed_sp = F)
```
